India's Prime Minister recently concluded a State Visit to Indonesia, an engagement that reinforced the India-Indonesia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. During the visit, the Prime Minister was conferred Indonesia's highest civilian honour, a recognition that marks a notable moment in bilateral ties.

The two countries share a history of cooperation on the world stage. Both played leading roles in the Bandung Conference of 1955, and both later became founding members of a group of states that are not formally aligned with any major power bloc. Their cooperation today spans several sectors. In defence, Indonesia agreed to procure an Indian supersonic cruise missile system. In maritime matters, the two countries agreed to develop a port near one of the world's busiest sea routes. Steel cooperation is also in place, with an Indian company agreeing to set up a manufacturing facility in Indonesia.

Cooperation extends to public health and disaster management as well. Regulators of the two countries agreed to strengthen cooperation on medical products, and the two countries' national agencies signed a memorandum on preparedness and response. In agriculture, India announced a supply of high-quality wheat seeds to Indonesia. Taken together, these steps show how a bilateral partnership can combine defence, industry, health and food security.

The 130th Constitution Amendment Bill, 2025, is one of three Bills tabled by the Home Minister, and a Joint Parliamentary Committee is currently examining it. The Bill responds to a situation in which a political office-holder continues in office while facing serious criminal charges. It proposes that a minister who is held in custody on such charges can be removed from office. The proposal reaches several categories of leaders. These include Union Ministers, State Ministers and Chief Ministers, and also the Chief Minister and Ministers of Delhi, Ministers of Union Territories and Ministers of Jammu & Kashmir. Each category is governed by its own legal basis, so the same principle is applied through different constitutional and statutory provisions. The Bill specifies who holds the removal power in each case, and, for Union Ministers, it also sets out what follows if the Prime Minister gives no advice. Some details of the removal process are linked to the length of custody and to the seriousness of the offence. The Bill has drawn criticism from those who fear that it could be misused against opposition-led governments. Supporters argue that it keeps leaders from retaining power while facing serious charges, which is a question of constitutional morality. Together, these rules make the Bill a detailed scheme for ministers facing criminal proceedings.

The Union Government has proposed an amendment to the National Food Security Act, 2013, that would change how foodgrains are allocated to households under the Antyodaya Anna Yojana. At present, each AAY household receives a fixed quantity of foodgrain each month, no matter how many members it has. The government argues that this household-based system creates inequities within the AAY category, because small households end up receiving more foodgrain per person than larger households. Under the proposal, the entitlement would be worked out for each individual in the household, with an overall ceiling for each household. The government expects this to make distribution more proportional to household size and to align allocation more closely with nutritional requirements. The change would also reduce disparities between AAY households and Priority Households. The amendment, however, does not deal with inclusion errors. The National Food Security Act was enacted to ensure food and nutritional security through subsidised foodgrains delivered by a targeted system. The households concerned belong to the poorest group within the Act. The proposal is still under consideration and is discussed here as a change in the making, so its final shape may differ from what is described above.

The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, known as CETA, is described as a next-generation free trade agreement. It goes beyond conventional tariff reduction and addresses market access, regulatory transparency and economic partnership. The scope of the deal is wide, covering trade in goods and services along with digital trade and investment. The framework also reaches government procurement, labour, environment, innovation, small and medium enterprises and regulatory cooperation. In this sense the agreement is broader than a simple list of duty cuts, since these areas show it addresses far more than goods moving across borders.

Tariff policy in the deal aims to balance two goals. Domestic industry is protected, while foreign goods gain access to the market in phases rather than all at once. Passenger vehicles show this balance clearly, since imports of these vehicles are handled through a quota arrangement.

The deal is also tied to predictability in trade. Countries are looking for stable and predictable trade relations amid geopolitical tensions and tariff disputes. A bilateral agreement offers a framework that reduces this uncertainty and supports long-term growth for both partners.

Taken together, these features show that the agreement combines tariff reduction with wider economic cooperation between the two countries.

Currency notes in India are usually printed on cotton-based banknote paper, but the Reserve Bank of India is now looking at a different material. The RBI has revived a proposal to introduce durable polymer-based banknotes, which are made from a specialised plastic material instead of paper. The Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited, a printing subsidiary wholly owned by the RBI, has invited global bids for a polymer substrate suitable for making such notes. Australia has already gone further, having introduced a complete series of polymer banknotes. Supporters of the idea point to the durability of plastic notes, which can withstand frequent use in circulation. The challenges, however, include cost, the need for new machines and the handling of plastic waste. The proposal therefore combines an old policy idea with a fresh push from the central bank. Polymer notes are therefore a topic of both economic and policy interest, since they involve printing, cost and environmental questions. The discussion covers the material, the printing arrangements and the financial trade-offs involved. Understanding how polymer notes are made, who prints them and what trade-offs they involve is useful for economic and current affairs preparation.

In July 2026, India and Japan held their 16th Annual Summit in New Delhi. The meeting came during the first official visit to India by Japan's Prime Minister, Sanae Takaichi, and it gave both governments a chance to review several areas of partnership at once. On defence, the two sides advanced a project connected with radio antenna technology and reached an agreement in principle on its remaining technical aspects. Leaders also decided to hold another high-level security dialogue later in the year, one that brings together senior ministers from both countries. On the economic front, the summit focused on secure and resilient supply chains. The two governments adopted a joint declaration covering strategic sectors, and they launched a cooperative programme linked to biogas and organic fertiliser, which fits India's wider energy goals. Trade and investment were also central to the talks. The two countries agreed to speed up the review of an existing trade pact, and they signed a memorandum that supports a major investment package. Finally, Japan offered support for India's plans to host a major United Nations conference on disaster risk reduction. This support carries forward the spirit of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction. Taken together, these outcomes show how the partnership now covers several sectors at once.

Sustainable development began as a defined concept before it became a set of global targets. A commission first defined the idea, and global meetings then built on that definition over the following decades. Early efforts focused on a small group of development goals. Later conferences followed up on these efforts, and they pushed the world to think beyond the original list. The eventual result was a broader framework covering poverty, health, education, gender equality, climate and peace. This framework was built as one agenda, with goals that were meant to be integrated with one another. Each annual review uses a score on a common scale, so that countries can be compared and their results can be read by policymakers and the public. Reviews of this kind are published every year, and they show how far each nation has moved toward the goals. Some regions have improved faster than others, while some targets have moved backwards, which shows that progress has been uneven. Looking back, the path from a concept to a framework took several decades and many meetings. Such a wide agenda made it possible to track progress across many different areas, even though it also made measurement more demanding.

India has inaugurated its first indigenously built hydrogen-powered train, which will run on a route connecting Jind and Sonipat in Haryana. The train is configured as a trainset of several coaches, and its power comes from a fuel cell propulsion system. Inside the train, fuel cells generate electricity through a reaction between hydrogen and oxygen. This electricity is not always used at once, so the surplus is stored in batteries for later use. The hydrogen itself is carried in cylinders that keep the gas compressed until the propulsion system needs it. Electric traction motors then convert electrical energy into mechanical energy, and this mechanical energy drives the train forward. The train's approved operating speed is set below its design speed, so it is allowed to run more slowly than it is built to run. Hydrogen is the lightest chemical element and is the most abundant element in the normal matter of the universe. Indian Railways has also introduced other technologies in recent years, including the KAVACH safety system and the Namo Bharat Rapid Rail. In short, the fuel cells are the source of power, the batteries store surplus power, the cylinders store the fuel, and the motors drive the train.

The monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds that brings significant changes in rainfall, and the word itself comes from an Arabic term meaning season. For India it is a major source of rain, because it supports agriculture, fills rivers, reservoirs, lakes and groundwater, and drives the national economy. A good monsoon usually means high crop yields and rising rural incomes, while a weak one can bring water shortages and crop failure. The southwest monsoon advances gradually across the country after its arrival in the south. It has two branches, which travel over different seas and reach different parts of the country. Mountains shape where rain falls: when moist air meets a barrier, it rises, cools and condenses. Ocean conditions far away can also change how strong the rains are. Monsoon behaviour is therefore not fixed, and in recent years experts have observed growing variability in its patterns, which makes planning for floods and droughts more important. Farmers, water managers and planners therefore watch the monsoon closely every year.

Many families spend a steady share of their income on electricity, and a rooftop solar programme offers one way to reduce that cost. The PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana is built around this idea. It encourages households to install solar panels on their rooftops so that the home can draw power from the sun. The scheme is described as the largest programme of its kind in the world, which reflects how many homes it is meant to reach. Because panels can be costly for ordinary families, the government offers financial support in the form of a subsidy that lowers the share of cost paid by each household. The basic goal is to give households free electricity up to a set number of units. The programme has also drawn outside finance. An international development bank has approved funds to support India's rooftop solar programme, which shows that the effort has attracted attention beyond the country. Alongside the household scheme, the government promotes a model solar village idea. Under this idea, villages are encouraged to become self-reliant in energy. Eligibility depends on population size, and special category states follow a lower threshold. Taken together, these measures link clean energy with everyday household life and with village-level independence. Such schemes also show how energy policy can reach households directly.

Foodgrain entitlements under the National Food Security Act are linked to categories of beneficiaries. Within the Antyodaya Anna Yojana, the present design gives a single fixed amount to each household, so the amount a person gets depends on how many people share the household. The Union Government has argued that this design produces inequities inside the category. A revised design would calculate the entitlement for each individual, while keeping a ceiling for each household so that large families do not receive unlimited grain. The government expects this to link allocation more closely with what people need to eat, and to make treatment across categories more uniform. The proposal does not, however, tackle one important concern in the system. Readers should remember that the amendment is still a proposal under discussion, and that its aims and limits are described in the booklet. The discussion covers the logic of the change and its effect on different households. The rules discussed here are a useful base for answering questions on this theme. Each part of the revised design is linked to a clear purpose, and the passage is meant to help a reader connect the purpose with the mechanism that the government has described for achieving it.

The Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail Corridor is a project between India and Japan. It links a city in Maharashtra with a city in Gujarat. The project draws on Shinkansen technology, and it forms part of India's National Rail Plan. The route passes through Gujarat, Maharashtra and Dadra and Nagar Haveli. Japan will supply train sets for the line, and one model, the E10, reflects a design partnership with a UK-based firm. Financing has come largely from Japan through a JICA loan that carries a very low interest rate. The implementing body is the National High-Speed Rail Corporation Limited. One stretch, between Surat and Bilimora, is scheduled to be completed before the rest of the corridor. India is expected to be the first country outside Japan to adopt one of the Shinkansen models that Japan will supply. The stations are located in both Gujarat and Maharashtra. The project is described as a flagship in the partnership between India and Japan. The completion of the entire corridor is scheduled for a later date than the Surat-Bilimora stretch. Taken together, the route, funding and train details show how the project combines Japanese technology with Indian infrastructure goals. The booklet gives several figures for distances, funding and timelines. Each of these points is drawn directly from the booklet's account of the project.

The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development was a major meeting held in Brazil, and it is widely remembered as the Earth Summit. Its central aim was to make the world see that environmental protection and sustainable development had to be pursued together. The conference adopted several documents. The first was a short statement of guiding principles, which stressed the precautionary approach, the polluter pays principle and common but differentiated responsibilities. The second was an action plan that was not legally binding, but it addressed poverty, sustainable consumption and the protection of fragile environments. This plan gave a stronger role to major groups such as women and indigenous people, and it offered a framework for action at local, national and global levels. The third document dealt with forests, and its principles were also not legally binding. These principles covered the conservation of forests and the sustainable management of all types of forests. Taken together, the outcomes of the conference laid part of the groundwork for later international agreements, including several that followed in the years after the summit. Many of these ideas were later revisited at summits held over the following decades, which kept the discussion active. Its outcomes were framed as guidance and action plans rather than as binding treaties.

A government policy framed in recent years changed the rules for India's space sector. It allowed non-government entities to take part across the complete space value chain. Several institutions now shape the sector, each with a distinct role. NewSpace India Limited is one of these bodies. Antrix Corporation is another body in this group, and it promotes space products, services and technologies. IN-SPACe acts as a single-window regulator for private space activities. It also runs a seed fund scheme that supports startups and MSMEs with grants. Foreign investment is governed separately by the FDI Policy, and the limits differ across segments. Satellite manufacturing and operations, launch vehicles and spaceports, and satellite components and subsystems are listed as separate segments. The limits therefore depend on the segment in which a company works. The segment rules guide foreign investment in each area. Private firms are now active in building launch vehicles and satellites. Recent examples of private work include Skyroot Aerospace, Cosmoserve Space and Cosmos Diamonds. Both government and private entities now operate within the same framework. Each institution has its own objectives and an office location. The sector now has a regulator, a commercial body and a marketing body. Together with the policy, these bodies shape how private firms enter India's space sector.

Railways came to India in the mid nineteenth century, when the first line was opened between two cities during the tenure of a Governor General. The network is now organised into administrative zones, and its tracks are of different widths. The country classifies these tracks into three groups based on the distance between the rails. Each zone manages a part of the national network. Some lines run through hilly terrain, and a few of them are known as mountain railways. In recent years, the government has focused on upgrading stations, raising speeds and adding safety systems. New high-speed trains have been introduced on several routes, including services with names such as Tejas and Humsafar. One long project links Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka. A financial arm supports the investment that such projects need. Several new schemes also aim at redeveloping stations and cutting energy use, which shows that the network is being modernised in many areas at once. Passenger services and station projects all depend on the same network, so planning must cover many needs at once. Track width is one of the ways the network's lines are described and compared. Several of these changes were announced in the same period, which shows the scale of the planned upgrades.

The World Bank sorts economies into four income groups using Atlas gross national income per capita, and it revises the cut-off values every year to account for global inflation. Thresholds are stated in current US dollars, and classifications remain in force for the financial year that begins on July 1. Because of this annual cycle, a country can move between groups as its economy grows or its figures are revised. The Atlas method averages exchange rates over several years, which softens the impact of short-term currency swings. The statistics ministry has launched a new monthly index that measures the real output of the formal services sector against a base year. It is the services counterpart of the index of industrial production, and it uses a fixed-weight method based on gross value added to remove the effect of price changes. The index covers formal service sub-sectors that account for a large share of the services economy. Data for April 2026 showed that most of these sub-sectors grew at double-digit rates. Investment flows also moved sharply. A UN agency report said that India's foreign direct investment inflows rose markedly in 2025, lifting India up the global rankings, even as worldwide flows stayed uneven. Indian companies also increased their overseas investment during the same year.

Scientists have raised safety concerns about a large hydropower project planned on a major river in Tibet. The concern arises from the local geology. The project's reservoir area is crossed by an active tectonic fault, which lies in the eastern Himalayan region of south-eastern Tibet. Such a fault is part of a larger fault system, and in this region that system is created by an ongoing collision between large tectonic plates. Because the fault is active, engineers must consider the possibility of movement near a dam that would hold back a great volume of water. The river itself is a major waterway that carries water from Tibet into South Asia. As it flows onward, it takes different names in different regions, passing through Indian states before it reaches the plains and crosses into the neighbouring country. Any decision to build a dam on its upper course therefore has effects far beyond the project site. Such a project should be judged carefully, with clear answers on the stability of the fault and the safety of nearby communities, before construction moves forward. Local residents and officials would need reliable information before any such decision is taken.

facts.title: Climate finance
facts.summary: Climate finance refers to financing from public, private or alternative sources that supports mitigation and adaptation against climate change. It rests on the Polluter Pays principle and CBDR-RC, and multilateral climate funds are coordinated by the UNFCCC. Persistent challenges include gaps between national needs and funding, slow approvals and much lower per-capita approved funding for Least Developed Countries.
facts: Climate finance: local, national or transnational financing for climate action
Sources: public, private or alternative financing
Principles: Polluter Pays, and Common but Differentiated Responsibility and Respective Capability (CBDR-RC)
Multilateral climate funds are coordinated by the UNFCCC
Global Environment Facility (GEF): operating entity of the financial mechanism (1994)
Adaptation Fund gives developing countries full ownership of adaptation projects
Clean Development Mechanism: emission-reduction projects in developing nations
Green Climate Fund estd. 2010 (COP 16), with LDCF and SCCF under it
Loss and Damage Fund (2023): financial assistance to nations most affected by climate change
Challenges: slow rate of approvals and gaps between national needs and NDC finance

facts.title: Indian Monsoon
facts.summary: The monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds that brings major changes in rainfall, and India receives about 75 per cent of its annual rainfall during it. The southwest monsoon runs from June to September and has an Arabian Sea branch and a Bay of Bengal branch. Jet streams influence the monsoon's onset, strength and withdrawal.
facts: Monsoon: a seasonal reversal of winds bringing significant changes in rainfall; word from Arabic 'Mausim' (season)
India receives about 75% of its annual rainfall during the monsoon
Southwest Monsoon: June to September; Northeast Monsoon: October to December
Arabian Sea branch strikes the Western Ghats and causes heavy rainfall on the west coast
Bay of Bengal branch moves towards Northeast India and brings rainfall to the Ganga plains
In summer, land heats faster than water: low pressure over N. India, high pressure over the Indian Ocean
Himalayas block cold Central Asian winds and force monsoon winds to shed moisture over India
Jet streams influence the onset, strength and withdrawal of the monsoon
El Nino (warming of Pacific Ocean waters) can weaken the Indian monsoon and reduce rainfall
Excess rainfall causes floods; weak monsoons lead to water shortages and droughts
